transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-05-02 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~58 min
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE); Priya Kapoor (Redwood SE); Jon Ruiz (Redwood Product); Emma Lopez (BrightDesk CTO); David Kim (BrightDesk ML Eng); Sara Thompson (BrightDesk PM); Ravi Anand (BrightDesk SRE)

Auto-summary: Demo of catalog curation + how benchmarks tie into model selection. Showed hardware compat matrix and how Optimize proposes quantization/batching. Customer requested trial Dedicated capacity and security follow-up.

Topics: Catalog upload, bench CSV format, mapping models to GPUs, prefix caching, cost-latency curves, rollout plan

Action items (refer to metadata for owners/dates)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex, I'm the AE on this account, with Priya our solutions engineer. Quick round - BrightDesk — is Emma still on?
[00:06] Emma (BrightDesk): Yep hey hi, Emma here. Thanks for scheduling, we've been excited to see how you do model selection at scale.
[00:12] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, quick agenda — we'll demo the catalog curation flow, show how to attach benchmark artifacts (CSV or S3), then walk the compatibility matrix that ties model variants to hardware and quantized kernels.
[00:20] David (BrightDesk): Good, our main use case is meeting summarization and short answer extraction. Latency matters for the UI, but cost is also a blocker.
[00:27] Sara (BrightDesk): And we have compliance constraints — some records must stay in our VPC for 90 days, so we need to see private deployment options.
[00:34] Alex (Redwood): Absolutely, we can cover private and Dedicated. Priya will show the Optimize suggestions for batching & quant so you can hit cost targets without big latency regressions.

[03:02] Priya (Redwood SE): Ok jumping in — here's the model catalog. Note: you can filter by task, seq length, and bench metric. We're uploading a sample bench CSV now (link shared in chat: https://redwood.app/s/bench-uploads/brightdesk-sample). The CSV schema is simple: model_id, seq_len, throughput, p95_lat_ms, tokens, prompt_type. We also accept JSON via the bench API.
[03:30] Ravi (BrightDesk): Quick q — does the CSV need the kernel mapping or do you infer it?
[03:36] Priya: Good question — we infer kernel mapping based on model architecture + your target GPU, but you can override to force a quantized kernel variant. That becomes part of the compatibility profile.

[06:15] Jon (Redwood Product): One nuance: for large seq lengths we recommend disabling certain fused-attention kernels on older Ampere cards — that shows up in the compatibility matrix as a red flag and a suggested fallback.

[08:50] David: We're interested in 16k and 32k context for some customers. How does Redwood handle KV cache memory across batch sizes?
[08:58] Priya: We show expected KV memory per request in the runtime profile. Optimize will flag if batching+KV would exceed SLOs and show you the break-even token price point. There's also prefix caching to avoid recomputing repeated system prompts.

[11:40] Emma: For the Dedicated trial, we want predictable tail latency. Do you provide p95 SLOs?
[11:47] Alex: Yes — Dedicated comes with configurable latency targets. We can set p90/p95 thresholds and alerting. If you want tighter SLAs we can discuss an enterprise add-on.

[14:05] Priya: Now demoing the compat matrix view. This is where models line up against "Hardware columns" — A100 80GB, H100, L40S, and a quantized CPU fallback. See how some open models are marked "Verified" vs "Compatible with cautions". That caution is based on kernel selection and observed p95 in our harness.
[14:40] Sara: Can we upload our own runner outputs from internal benchmarks? We run a few tokenizers differently, so numbers won't match yours exactly.
[14:49] Priya: Yes, you can import runner outputs. We normalize tokenizer differences by recording token counts and the prompt_type. The UI lets you pin your bench as the canonical metric for your workspace so rollouts reference your numbers.

[18:12] David: Is there a way to automate model selection per route? Like pick cheaper variant if latency under X?
[18:19] Priya: Yep, smart routing policies. You configure rules: prefer lowest cost under latency threshold, fallback to more expensive model for sub-100ms remaining time budget, region-aware routing too. We surfaced a few examples in the walkthrough.

[21:05] Alex: Quick pause for questions — anything on security?
[21:12] Emma: SOC 2 is big for us. Do you provide audit logs for prompt-level access and KMS integration for private keys?
[21:20] Priya: We integrate with most KMS/HSM providers and retain audit logs in the customer Console. For Private deployments the customer controls KMS. We'll scope exact controls in the security review.

[25:00] Priya: Switching to Optimize panel — here we show recommended quantization + batch sizes per model for your workload signature. For example, for a 2k average context we recommended int8-quant on L40S with batch size 4 to hit 40% cost savings while keeping p95 under 350ms. We annotated expected quality delta from internal evals — usually small for summarization workloads.

[27:30] Ravi: Can we opt for automatic rollouts using those suggestions? We have a canary process.
[27:36] Jon: Yes, the rollout engine supports canaries and A/B. You can tie rollback to quality regression thresholds or token-cost spikes.

[30:10] Emma: A practical question — we have an on-prem cluster for PHI workloads. How different is the private package?
[30:18] Priya: Private includes a customer-managed control plane and on-prem deployable runtime. The runtime is the same code path but with network isolation and optional air-gap packaging. We will need to validate kernel compatibility for your GPUs on your infra — that's part of the onboarding checklist.

[34:02] David: About benchmarks — you mentioned 'verified' models. How often are those re-run and how do you account for new kernel patches?
[34:10] Priya: We run a nightly harness for top models across our supported hardware. Kernel patches can change perf; we flag major deltas and regenerate the compatibility signal. If a patch impacts performance we annotate with the patch version in the matrix.

[37:45] Alex: We're going to show importing a bench now — watch how the catalog tags models and auto-suggests a shortlist. (screen share) You can click a model and see pinned bench artifacts and the per-route cost estimate.
[38:10] Sara: The cost estimates — are those per-token or per-request?
[38:14] Priya: Per-token (input + output). We show both token breakout and amortized infra cost for Dedicated. For Dedicated we show unit cost after committed utilization and any oversub pricing.

[42:00] David: Suppose we pick a model that is cheap on A100 but H100 is our primary infra. Is there a migration path?
[42:08] Priya: Migrations are handled by rerunning a quick kernel mapping pass and re-benchmarking the model variant on H100. The Console has a 'remap to hardware' button that queues a small bench job. We can also run a targeted QA run as part of the trial.

[46:20] Emma: One of our concerns is hallucination on summarization. Does Redwood hook into evals or can we plug in our own prompts/eval sets?
[46:27] Jon: Yes — you can upload eval suites, tie them to rollouts, and get regression alerts. We support both qualitative metrics (ROUGE, BLEU) and custom checks that look for hallucination patterns.

[49:55] Alex: Nearing the end — quick recap: we'll provision a 2-week Dedicated trial, Priya will run a BrightDesk-targeted summarization bench (you'll share a sample dataset or prompt pack), Alex will send pricing and trial terms, and we'll schedule a security call to go over SOC2/KMS details.

[50:20] Emma: Sounds good. For the trial can we get access to the bench runner code so we can reproduce?
[50:26] Priya: Yes, we'll share the runner and a script to post results to the bench API. Expect a GitHub link in the follow-up.

[52:40] Ravi: Two quick nitpicks: one, tokenizer mismatch between our BPE and your baseline; two, we need to validate tail p99 on our real traffic shape.
[52:50] Priya: Noted — tokenizer mismatch is why we normalize by token counts and allow you to pin your own bench. For p99 we can do a load-run on your trace; that's part of the trial scope.

[55:15] Sara: Ok last thing — any third-party cost for inference libs we should be aware of? i.e., license for quant libs?
[55:22] Jon: We rely on open runtimes and some vendor-provided kernels; licensing is usually permissive for inference. We'll list any vendor-specific constraints in the onboarding doc.

[57:10] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the links and action items.
[57:16] Emma: Thanks, this was useful.

End of transcript
